chapter_theme: The second half of the hunters' vari: songs that see the goddess dance her victory and walk before the cattle raider, three songs that show the seized herds filling the yards of smith, bards, toddy seller, augur and elders, and stanzas offering her blood and bali as the hunters' due while praising her as Siva's consort and Mal's kin; it closes by wishing the vetchi on the Pandya of Pothiyil.

cast.role: the hunters (Maravar) of the forest beside the Aiyai shrine, who sing the vari
the goddess of victory (Aiyai, Kumari, Neeli) worshipped by the hunters
a young hunter woman addressed in the songs of the seized herds
the woman who sells toddy to the hunters

silappathikaram:12:116-119.reading: The hunters sing that the goddess, her fine anklets, wristlets and girdle ringing, seems to dance the victory sword-dance on stilts as the deceiving asuras fall, and that the gods, praising her body dark as the kaya flower, seem to shower flowers from their hands.
silappathikaram:12:116-119.nuance: Every line ends in போலும் (it seems): the singers describe the costumed girl of the rite as if she were the goddess dancing her battle, so the song is a seeing-as rather than a report. The dance on stilts (மரக்கால்) over the falling asuras is the myth's dance of victory; the dark body (காயா மலர்மேனி) ties her to Mal, whose younger kin the first half of the kaathai calls her.
silappathikaram:12:116-119.event: The goddess dances on stilts as the asuras fall and the gods shower flowers on her.

silappathikaram:12:120-123.reading: When a man of the small village inside the forest sets out to seize cattle, the goddess who plies the white sword seems to want to wear the vetchi flower too, and if she does, the kaari bird in the enemy village's forest seems to cry its harsh omen.
silappathikaram:12:120-123.nuance: The goddess takes the raider's own badge, the vetchi flower of cattle seizure, so the raid becomes her act; the omen bird crying in the enemy's grove (கட்சி) is the sign of their loss. The song turns on condition (வேண்டின்): her wish is what makes the omen fall.
silappathikaram:12:120-123.event: A hunter sets out to seize cattle and the goddess takes the vetchi with him while an omen bird cries in the enemy's grove.

claims.claim: the goddess takes up the raider's vetchi, and her will shows itself in omens over the enemy's land

silappathikaram:12:124-127.reading: When the woman who sells toddy refuses him, the warrior who cannot bear it takes his bow and goes, with birds leading the way, to seize the cattle of his foes, and as he goes the goddess of victory seems to raise her banner and walk before his bow.
silappathikaram:12:124-127.nuance: The raid starts from a small want: the toddy seller will not pour (மறுப்ப), so the hunter goes for cattle to pay her. The song sets this trade motive and the goddess's banner side by side without embarrassment; the birds on the road (புள்ளும் வழிப்படர) are the omens of the way.
silappathikaram:12:124-127.event: Refused toddy by the toddy seller, a hunter takes his bow and goes to raid cattle, and the goddess goes before him with her banner.

claims.claim: the goddess of victory walks before the raider's bow when he goes for the enemy's cattle

silappathikaram:12:128-131.reading: The singers bid the young hunter woman look: the fine herds her brothers brought back from yesterday's raid now fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the skilled yazh-playing bards.
silappathikaram:12:128-131.nuance: The spoil is not kept: it goes at once to the craftsmen and musicians of the raid (the smith who makes the weapons, the துடி drummer, the bards). The address to the girl (இளமா எயிற்றி) makes her the witness of her brothers' valour shown as giving.
silappathikaram:12:128-131.event: The herds seized in the raid are given out and fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the bards.

silappathikaram:12:132-135.reading: Again the young woman is bidden to look: the herds her brothers seized while the karanthai men cried out fill the yards of the toddy seller, the forest man who picks good bamboo, and the augur who read the bird omen.
silappathikaram:12:132-135.nuance: The list pays the debts of the raid one by one: the toddy seller who refused credit in lines 124-127 is now paid in cattle, and the augur (கணி) is paid for the omen that sent them out. கரந்தை here names the defenders of the herd by their flower.
silappathikaram:12:132-135.event: The seized herds fill the yards of the toddy seller, the bamboo-cutter and the augur.

silappathikaram:12:136-140.reading: A third time the young woman is bidden to look: the herds her brothers drove off while the neighbouring village wailed fill the yards of the grey-bearded old Eyinar and Eyinar women, and a rubric marks the songs to the goddess that follow.
silappathikaram:12:136-140.nuance: The third song ends with the elders of the hunters' own kin; the neighbouring village's wail (அயலூர் அலற) is the price, stated plainly. Line 138 (நயனில் மொழியின்) is hard: it may describe the old men's rough speech; the sense is not secure. Line 140, துறைப்பாட்டுமடை, is a rubric, not a verse line.
silappathikaram:12:136-140.event: The herds seized from a neighbouring village fill the yards of the old Eyinar men and women.

silappathikaram:12:141-144.reading: The hunters say they worship the goddess's paired feet, which grant grace to the sages and gods who wander with the sun so their distress ends, and that this is the due the mighty Eyinar owe as they touch her feet: blood flowing from the throat, the price of the victory she gives.
silappathikaram:12:141-144.nuance: The hymn joins the goddess's grace (அருளும்) and the price of blood (விலையே) in one stanza: victory is a purchase and blood the payment. Whose throat bleeds is not said: an animal's, a captive's, or the hunters' own offered blood; I leave it open.
silappathikaram:12:141-144.event: The hunters touch the goddess's feet and offer throat-blood as their due for victory.

claims.claim: the victory the goddess grants is bought with blood offered to her as the hunters' due

silappathikaram:12:145-148.reading: The hunters worship her flower feet, jewel-formed, to which the crowned gods and their king bow, and say this is the due offered by the victorious Eyinar who come in a full band: blood with fat dripping from it, the price that crushes their rivals.
silappathikaram:12:145-148.nuance: The second stanza repeats the first's frame (தொழுதேம் ... கடனிது ... விலையே) with the gods' king in place of the sages, and fat (நிணன்) added to the blood: the offering is flesh as well as blood.
silappathikaram:12:145-148.event: The hunters offer blood and fat at the goddess's feet as the price of victory over rivals.

silappathikaram:12:149-152.reading: The Eyinar who come bursting out at midnight like killing tigers, with drum, small drum and horn sounding, touch the maiden goddess's feet, and this, they say, is the due they owe: the offering of food at the head of the bali.
silappathikaram:12:149-152.nuance: The night raid and the night offering are the same band in the same noise: the drums that sound for the attack (வெடிபட வருபவர்) sound for the rite. படுகடன், the debt that has fallen due, makes the bali an obligation rather than a gift.
silappathikaram:12:149-152.event: The hunters come at midnight with drums and lay the bali at the goddess's feet.

claims.claim: the bali is a debt the hunters owe the goddess, not a gift they may withhold

silappathikaram:12:153-156.reading: The hunters pray that travellers may multiply and the road grow rich, and ask the goddess, Sankari, Antari, Neeli, who sets the red-eyed snake and the crescent on her matted crown, to eat the due of the Eyinar of strong bows and arrows.
silappathikaram:12:153-156.nuance: To a highway robber a road rich with travellers (வம்பலர் பல்கி) is a rich harvest: the prayer for safe, busy roads is, from these singers, a prayer for prey. The goddess carries Siva's snake and crescent, so the hymn makes her his consort.

silappathikaram:12:157-160.reading: They ask her to eat the due of the pitiless Eyinar who fall on sleeping villages with the startling drum, and praise her who, while the gods who ate nectar still die, ate the poison none would eat and sits granting grace.
silappathikaram:12:157-160.nuance: Two contrasts are packed together: the gods who drank amrita still die, while she who drank poison lives and gives grace; and the hunters who have no eyes for pity (கண்ணில்) are fed by her grace. The poison-swallowing is Siva's act; the hymn gives it to the goddess as his other half.

silappathikaram:12:161-164.reading: They ask her to eat the due of the graceless Eyinar, who show no mercy to anyone but take his goods and wound him, and praise her who walked between the marutham trees and kicked to pieces the rolling cart of deceit her uncle sent.
silappathikaram:12:161-164.nuance: The singers call themselves அருளில் (without grace) in the same stanza that praises the goddess's grace (அருள் செய்குவாய்); the hymn does not ask her to change them, only to eat their due. The feats of the marutham trees and the cart sent by the uncle are Krishna's, given to her as Mal's kin.

silappathikaram:12:165-168.reading: The vari closes with a blessing: may the hill-lord of high Pothiyil, mighty and eager for victory, wear the vetchi so that the groves and karanthai of other lands go to ruin.
silappathikaram:12:165-168.nuance: The hunters' raid becomes the king's war: the vetchi they wore for cattle is wished on the Pandya, the lord of Pothiyil, unnamed here. Line 165 (மறைமுது முதல்வன் பின்னர் மேய) is obscure: it may set the king after an ancient first lord, but the reference cannot be fixed. The kaathai that hailed Kannaki as the goddess ends by praying for the victory of the king who will die before her word.

links.note: Both tie the cattle raid to toddy: in the Purananuru the jar is kept for the raider who will bring a herd; here the toddy seller's refusal sends the hunter out.
links.teaches: Read together they show toddy as the raid's credit: the poem's kept jar is advance pay, and the epic's refusal is the unpaid debt the seized herd later settles in the seller's yard.

gains.a: the epic's brief motive (a refused drink) gains the Sangam custom behind it, where the raider is paid in toddy before he goes
gains.b: the Purananuru poem gains the other side of the trade: a seller who will not pour and is paid afterwards in cattle (lines 132-135)

links.note: The Purananuru raider takes herds yet his own pot shows no curd; the epic names whose yards the seized herds fill.
links.teaches: The poem's pitied raider who keeps nothing is explained by the epic's list: the herd goes to smith, drummer, bards, augur and toddy seller, so a raid's wealth is a gift economy that leaves the raider poor.

gains.a: the list of yards gains its point: giving the herd away is the raider's honour, as the poem's empty curd-pot shows
gains.b: the poem's riddle (why a cattle-taker has no curd) gains the epic's answer in named receivers

links.note: The hunters pay for victory with blood at the goddess's feet; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations.
links.teaches: The conflict is about what an offering is worth: the hymn makes killing itself the price that buys the goddess's favour, while the couplet holds that no offering outweighs one life spared; it holds if the throat-blood of line 144 is a slain creature's.

gains.a: the hymn's blood price gains a measure from outside the cult, one by which the payment is a loss
gains.b: the couplet's comparison of oblation and abstention gains a live case where the offering is not ghee but blood

links.note: The hunters owe the goddess a bali as a debt; Tirumular, having nothing to show the god who eats oblations, offers a song as his food offering.
links.teaches: The vari is itself a song sung over the bali, so the hunters give both the blood and the song that Tirumular offers in its place, which shows the song offering was a companion of the blood rite before it was a substitute for it.

gains.a: the hunters' debt-offering gains a contrast that shows its song as a second offering, not mere accompaniment
gains.b: Tirumular's song-oblation gains a scene of the older rite in which song and blood were offered together

links.note: Tirumular praises the lord who swallowed the poison and shares half his body with the lady; the hunters give the poison-swallowing to the goddess herself.
links.teaches: The hymn moves Siva's defining act of grace to his consort through the shared body Tirumular names, and makes it the ground on which a goddess who eats the pitiless hunters' offerings still grants grace.

gains.a: the hymn's attribution gains its basis: the goddess is the half of the poison-eater's body
gains.b: Tirumular's half-body formula gains a use outside Saiva devotion, where it lets a forest goddess claim Siva's deed

links.note: The Kural says wealth that comes without grace and love should be let go; the hunters name themselves graceless takers of wealth by wounding and ask the gracious goddess to eat their due.
links.teaches: Where the couplet tells the getter to let graceless wealth roll away, the hymn shows a community whose living is exactly such wealth offering a share of it to a goddess of grace, who is asked not to refuse it; the tension rests on reading the due as paid from the plunder.

gains.a: the hunters' self-description gains the ethical name for what they live by: wealth that comes without arul
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case where graceless wealth is not let go but sanctified by offering

links.note: The hunters close their rite praying that the Pandya of Pothiyil wear the vetchi and ruin other lands; in Madurai the same king's sceptre fails and he falls dead before Kannaki.
links.teaches: The blessing asks for victory over others' lands, but the king's ruin comes from within his own court; the forest rite that hailed Kannaki as the goddess has, unknowing, blessed the king she will undo.

new_concepts.gloss: the offering of blood or food laid before a fierce deity as a due owed to her
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's word: பலிமுக மடை (Silappathikaram 12, line 152); the hymns also call it கடன் and விலை

source_issues: silappathikaram:12:136-140: line 140, துறைப்பாட்டுமடை, is a rubric introducing the following stanzas but is counted as a verse line of the last herd song.
The kaathai header reports a printed last line of 70 against 168 counted lines; the numbering here follows show.

silappathikaram:12:153-156 to 161-164: the three stanzas are counted as three 4-line units though each pairs a refrain line (உண்குவாய்) with a praise line (செய்குவாய்/சேர்த்துவாய்); the boundaries look right.
